title: Newspaper pages: are the mean and the median close?
description: A week of newspaper page counts has a mean and a median that nearly agree, and the board compares them with the family heights and the stories read. Keeko doubts that the mean is always the bigger one.
teaching_notes: One idea: mean and median are both measures of central tendency; they agree when the data is balanced and part when an outlier pulls one way. Watch for children who think the mean is always above the median.

source: A newspaper had 16, 18, 20, 22, 26, 16 and 10 pages from Mon
video_script.why: The child has seen a low outlier and a high outlier and now meets balanced data.
video_script.substitution: When values spread evenly on both sides, the mean and the median meet near the middle.
video_script.wrong_answer: the mean is always bigger than the median
video_script.wrong_move: says the mean is always the bigger one because that happened with the stories, but not with the family heights
video_script.payoff_line: Mean and median are close because the data is balanced

final_answer.spoken: the mean is about eighteen point two nine pages and the median is eighteen pages

names.Ruhee: family whose heights include one short member

hold_back: Mean and median are close because the data is balanced
maths_rules: mean and median are measures of central tendency
video_script.design: One idea: compare the mean and the median. A week of newspapers stays in the anchor; the pages sort; then three data sets line up for comparison.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>A newspaper has a different number of pages on different days of the week.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The pages from Monday to Sunday are marked on the newspapers.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>How will the mean and the median of these pages compare?

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

marks.g1: the mean mark and the median mark each point at the centre of a group of dots

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>The mean and the median each give one number for the centre of the data.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the mean and the median, and see how close they are.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, mean = total ÷ number of days: total 128; 128 ÷ 7 ≈ 18.29 pages

marks.s1: the rule mean = total ÷ number of days is written
marks.s2: the seven counts add up to 128

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, add the pages of all seven days and share the total.
<bookmark mark='s2'/>The total is one hundred and twenty eight pages.
<bookmark mark='s3'/>Divided by seven days, the mean is about eighteen point two nine.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, median: sorted 10, 16, 16, 18, 20, 22, 26; the 4th value is 18

marks.d2: the sorted counts are shown in a row
marks.d3: the 4th count, 18, is circled with three on each side

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Step two, sort the pages from smallest to largest.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>Ten, sixteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, twenty two and twenty six.
<bookmark mark='d3'/>There are seven values, so the fourth one has three on each side.
The median is eighteen pages.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, compare: mean 18.29 and median 18 are very close; no value is far from the rest

marks.e2: the two marks sit almost on top of each other
marks.e3: the seven dots lie evenly on both sides of the marks

narration: <bookmark mark='e1'/>Step three, compare the mean and the median.
<bookmark mark='e2'/>Eighteen point two nine and eighteen are very close.
<bookmark mark='e3'/>No value pulls the mean far away, so the dots lie evenly on both sides.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, compare with the earlier examples: Ruhee's family, low outlier, mean 160.2 below median 170; stories, high outlier, mean 8.13 above median 6

marks.f1: the three data sets line up in three rows
marks.f2: in Ruhee's row the mean mark sits left of the median mark
marks.f3: in the stories row the mean mark sits right of the median mark

narration: <bookmark mark='f1'/>Step four, compare with the two earlier examples.
<bookmark mark='f2'/>Ruhee's family had a low outlier, so the mean was below the median.
<bookmark mark='f3'/>The stories had a high outlier, so the mean was above the median.

beats.on_screen: Answer: mean ≈ 18.29 pages and median 18 pages, close because the data is balanced
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Mean and median are close because the data is balanced.
The mean is about eighteen point two nine pages, and the median is eighteen pages.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's thought bubble shows the mean mark always on the right of the median mark; then Ruhee's row shows the mean mark on the left and the bubble is struck through

marks.fix: Ruhee's row is shown with the mean mark on the left of the median mark

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the mean is always bigger than the median, like it was with the stories.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>With Ruhee's family, the mean was smaller than the median.
<bookmark mark='idea'/>Which is bigger depends on which side the far value lies.
